title: Audit Binary Stream Cipher Service
scenario: A security engineer is auditing an internal log-shipping service written in Go. The service uses a compiled binary plugin (`/app/lib/encryptor.so`, a CGo shared library with no source) to encrypt audit log entries before writing them to disk. The Go service source (~1,200 lines across 6 files) is present, but the encryption plugin is opaque. A corpus of ~50,000 encrypted log files from production is available in `/app/data/logs/`. The service has a self-test mode that encrypts known plaintexts. The security team suspects the keystream has a structural weakness, and needs a decryptor written as a Go tool at `/app/tools/decrypt/main.go` that can recover all plaintext log entries.
instruction_draft: The service at `/app/` encrypts audit log entries using a compiled plugin at `/app/lib/encryptor.so` before writing them to `/app/data/logs/`. Write a Go tool at `/app/tools/decrypt/main.go` that reads any encrypted log file produced by this service and writes the recovered plaintext to stdout. Running `go run /app/tools/decrypt/main.go /app/data/logs/<file>` must produce the correct original plaintext. Your tool must also correctly decrypt the files placed at `/app/verify/inputs/` at verification time and write each result to `/app/verify/outputs/<filename>.txt`.
requirements: A Go source file exists at `/app/tools/decrypt/main.go` and compiles with `go build`.
Running the tool on any file in `/app/data/logs/` produces the correct plaintext (verifiable via embedded HMAC or known-prefix check in each log entry).
Running the tool on each file in `/app/verify/inputs/` produces the correct plaintext written to `/app/verify/outputs/<filename>.txt`.
The tool handles all entry lengths present in the corpus (1–4096 bytes of plaintext per entry).
The tool must not call the `encryptor.so` plugin itself to decrypt (verified by strace at check time).
environment: A Go service in `/app/` with files: `main.go`, `logger/logger.go`, `logger/rotate.go`, `plugin/loader.go`, `config/config.go`, `internal/util.go`. The service loads `/app/lib/encryptor.so` via cgo dlopen, calls `encrypt_entry(key_id uint32, nonce []byte, plaintext []byte) []byte`.

`/app/lib/encryptor.so`: a compiled CGo shared library (no source). Exports: `encrypt_entry`. The plugin implements a custom 32-bit LFSR-based keystream XOR cipher. The LFSR polynomial is x^32+x^22+x^2+x^1+1 (a standard Galois LFSR). The seed is derived as `seed = key_id XOR crc32(nonce)`. The keystream is generated byte-by-byte from the LFSR output LSBs. The nonce (16 bytes) and key_id (4 bytes, little-endian) are prepended to the ciphertext in each encrypted file, followed by a 4-byte little-endian plaintext length, then the ciphertext bytes.
The service config at `/app/config/config.yaml` contains a `key_id` field (a uint32). The service generates a random 16-byte nonce per log entry using `crypto/rand`.

`/app/data/logs/` contains 50,000 encrypted log files generated by running the service against a synthetic plaintext corpus. Each file: 4 bytes key_id (LE) + 16 bytes nonce + 4 bytes plaintext_len (LE) + N bytes ciphertext.
The service has a `--selftest` flag that encrypts a hardcoded 64-byte known plaintext and prints hex of the result to stdout, useful for probing.
A self-test runner script `/app/selftest.sh` that calls the service in selftest mode with varying key_ids and prints results.

Verification directory `/app/verify/inputs/` is empty at setup time; the verifier plants 20 fresh encrypted files at check time using a separate invocation of the service (different key_ids and nonces, all drawn from the same LFSR/key_id/nonce derivation logic).
An output directory `/app/verify/outputs/` exists and is empty.
The Go module is initialized (`go.mod` present) with module path `audit-service`.
The compiled `encryptor.so` exports only `encrypt_entry`; no decrypt export exists. `nm` and `objdump` will show symbol names but not source.
internal_hint: Difficulty comes from two interacting levers: (1) opaque_component — the LFSR cipher lives entirely inside the compiled `.so` with no source; the solver must characterize it by experiment (probe `--selftest` with known plaintexts, vary key_id/nonce, XOR known plaintext against ciphertext to recover keystream, observe period and structure); (2) build_component — once the LFSR polynomial and seed derivation are reverse-engineered, the solver must implement a correct Go decryptor that handles the full seed derivation (`key_id XOR crc32(nonce)`), LFSR stepping (Galois form, correct tap mask `0x80200003`), and byte extraction. The tricky correctness condition: the LFSR outputs a 32-bit word per step but only the LSB is used per byte, so 8 LFSR steps are needed per output byte — naive implementations that use the full word mod 256 or take one bit per byte from a single step will produce wrong keystreams on inputs longer than a few bytes. This is invisible from the sample data unless the solver tests on entries longer than 32 bytes AND verifies byte-by-byte. The verification inputs include entries of lengths 1, 7, 31, 32, 33, 64, 128, 255, 256, 512, 1024, 4096 to catch off-by-one and period bugs.
trap: A naive solver XORs the keystream recovered from a short known-plaintext (e.g., the 64-byte selftest) and hardcodes that stream, or implements the LFSR but takes the full 32-bit output word modulo 256 per byte instead of one bit per step. Both approaches produce correct output for the first 32 bytes or for entries that happen to be short, but silently diverge on entries longer than 32 bytes. Since many log files in the sample corpus are short, shallow verification against the sample passes; the hidden verify-time inputs include entries of 256, 512, and 4096 bytes which expose the divergence.
tests: Self-consistency on sample: for 50 randomly selected files from `/app/data/logs/`, run the tool and verify the output starts with the known log prefix string `LOG_ENTRY:` (embedded in every plaintext by the logger).

HMAC integrity: each plaintext ends with a 32-byte HMAC-SHA256 tag over `key_id || nonce || plaintext_body` using a fixed audit HMAC key stored in `/app/config/config.yaml`; verifier checks HMAC validity on 50 sample files.

Verify-time inputs (20 fresh files planted by verifier): for each file in `/app/verify/inputs/`, check that `/app/verify/outputs/<filename>.txt` exists, starts with `LOG_ENTRY:`, and passes the HMAC integrity check.
Long-entry correctness: verify-time inputs include files with plaintext lengths 256, 512, 1024, and 4096 bytes; HMAC check must pass for all.
No plugin call: `strace -e trace=openat,dlopen go run /app/tools/decrypt/main.go /app/verify/inputs/<file>` must not show a dlopen/openat of `encryptor.so`.
Varied key_id: verify-time inputs use 5 distinct key_id values (including key_id=0, key_id=1, key_id=0xFFFFFFFF, and two random values); HMAC must pass for all.

verifier_knob.name: number of verify-time input files and length distribution
verifier_knob.value: 20 files spanning 7 distinct lengths and 5 key_ids
verifier_knob.effect: Raising to 50 files with more lengths/key_ids catches more subtle LFSR implementation bugs (e.g., wrong tap polynomial, off-by-one in nonce CRC, endianness of key_id); lowering to 5 short-only files makes the task easier since short-entry bugs are less likely.

expected_failure_modes: Agent correctly identifies the LFSR structure but uses the wrong tap mask (e.g., confuses Galois vs Fibonacci form), producing wrong keystreams for all but trivially short entries.
Agent gets the LFSR right but derives the seed incorrectly (e.g., uses `key_id + crc32(nonce)` instead of XOR, or uses big-endian key_id), causing all verify-time decryptions to fail.
Agent implements LFSR outputting one full 32-bit word per byte (mod 256) rather than one bit per step, passing short-entry tests but failing the 256+ byte entries.

Agent calls `encryptor.so` indirectly (wraps it in a subprocess) to decrypt by trying all nonces — impossible since nonce is 16 bytes — or tries to build a decryption export into the shared library; fails because the plugin has no decrypt path and `strace` check catches any `.so` open.
Agent reverse-engineers the cipher correctly but writes the output files to the wrong path or with wrong filename, failing the state-check even with correct decryption logic.
